newsitem.title: FRANCE: McQueen's debut show disappoints fashion crowd.
newsitem.headline: McQueen's debut show disappoints fashion crowd.

text.p: Hopes that Briton Alexander McQueen would put Givenchy back on fashion's cutting edge were abruptly deflated on Sunday when the designer sent out a theatrical, antiquity-inspired collection that ressembled a costume ball.
The muscle-bound blond god that looked down from on high, bow and arrow in hand, and the maiden strumming her harp had announced a poetic neo-classical fashion voyage.

But instead of showing off the brilliant tailoring he acquired during his years as an apprentice on Savile Row, McQueen, in his debut collection for Givenchy, put on a bizarre spectacle of large hairdos, gold-tinted breasts spilling from rib-crushing corsets and has-been snake-skin trenchcoats.

But talent McQueen does have and at times it leaped out from the gold and white mythical masquerade like an electric spark: draped chiffon birth-of-Venus dresses wound with ivy, a snowy brocade dress with billowing sleeves or an opera coat, its back painted like an Italian fresco.
However it is difficult to imagine Givenchy's prim and proper clientele wearing McQueen's gladiator tunics and pheasant-feather body suits to a charity luncheon.

"It was spectacular and full of creativity. I don't think it was about wearability but he has enormous talent," said Dawn Mello, president of Bergdorf-Goodman. "He wanted to make a statement about change. I think it's unfair to judge a designer by his first collection."

Earlier in the day, chiffons in shades of a sunset over Bora-Bora or the waters of a Tahitian lagoon swirled down the catwalk at French designer Rosette Torrente-Mette's summery haute couture collection.
A statuesque woman performing Polynesian dance and "natives" handing out jasmine flowers set the stage for the feminine collection gleaned from exotic island flora and fauna.
There were plenty of ostrich-skin coats in beige, dusty rose and lime, orange suede dresses and tunics embroidered with eyelet lace, and canary-coloured hide trousers.
From the demure Jackie Kennedy suits of lacquered irridescent brocade to the New Look crinoline petticoats, it was gay and ladylike, if short on modernity and innovation.

"I would say it was a superb collection which has the advantage of being wearable. Rosette Mette understands perfectly the needs of an active woman," smiled former French Socialist Prime Minister Edith Cresson.
But the black-clad actress Marisa Berenson felt differently.

"It was a glamorous collection but for myself I prefer no colour. I like black, beige," she said. "But it is a summer collection, so I suppose the pastels were right. I do like to wear them on the beach."
French couturiers have been desperately searching for themes to give their collections focus to counter a dwindling customer base and the increasing prominence of foreign designers.
Frenchman Olivier Lapidus gleaned inspiration from Mother Nature herself, composing an "ecological premiere...joining luxury and agricultural products".

Lapidus said he had crafted the clothes from vegetable fibres, creating such textiles as "doupion based on mint, satin organdies mixed with blackcurrant, silk jersey and daisies, grapevine leaves or raspberry".
